corpus: the repository itself; every target is a project-relative path
how_it_was_made: Each pair was written by reading the file and asking what a user would type to find it.
The target was written down before anything was run, and the semantic search was never consulted while writing.
Targets name the file that defines or implements the thing asked about. A test or an answer key is a target only when the question is about the test or the rule itself.
Class A and C questions are natural sentences. They are not padded with rare words to force FTS to zero -- FTS puts an implicit AND between quoted terms, so an ordinary question already misses.

Eight rewrites across seven questions were made after the validator caught them: the class is defined mechanically as "FTS scores zero" (R3), so a question that happened to share every word with some file was mislabelled rather than merely awkward. The target never moved, only the wording, and the vector layer was still not consulted. Four of the seven were Norwegian questions matching TODO.md -- 1200 lines of Norwegian prose contain most ordinary Norwegian words, which is itself worth knowing about this corpus.

Class C targets are English files only, on purpose. This corpus describes the same mechanisms in Norwegian prose (TODO.md, tests/gold/FASIT-*.md), so a Norwegian question that those files also answer cannot measure crossing the language boundary. A Norwegian document ranked above the code counts as a miss here, and that is the point of the class.

classes.A: true paraphrase, English question, English file. FTS must score 0.
classes.B: lexical: the words are in the file. FTS must score at least one hit.
classes.C: cross-language: Norwegian question, English file. FTS must score 0.
